title: Indian-American Student Says Campus Reform Dropped Him After Anti-Bigotry Vote
excerpt: Vasant Bhatt, 21, says his senior correspondent role was terminated after he voted for a Democrat in Texas to protest anti-Indian bigotry. Campus Reform has not commented publicly.
body:
• Vasant Bhatt, 21, a University of Houston political science student, says Campus Reform has terminated his role as a senior correspondent.
  • Bhatt says the move followed his public statement that he voted for Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in Texas's US Senate race to protest anti-Indian bigotry.
  • Campus Reform has not commented publicly on his claim; his author profile, which listed him as a Senior Correspondent, no longer appears on the site.
  • Bhatt previously interned with Senator Ted Cruz's re-election campaign — his break is with his own side of politics, which is why the case is drawing attention ahead of the November 3 midterms.

A 21-year-old Indian-American student journalist in Texas says Campus Reform, the conservative higher-education outlet, has ended his role as a correspondent after he publicly said he voted for a Democrat to protest anti-Indian bigotry. Vasant Bhatt, a political science student at the University of Houston, announced the move in a post on X on Friday, according to IANS reporting carried by multiple outlets.

"I exercised my constitutional right to vote according to my conscience, spoke out against anti-Indian bigotry, and refused to toe the Republican Party line. My participation in Campus Reform's correspondent program has now been terminated."

— Vasant Bhatt, in a post on X

Bhatt added that losing the place would not make him retract his beliefs or abandon his community. His claim is, at this stage, his account: Campus Reform has not commented publicly, and IANS reports that his online profile page — which described him as a Senior Correspondent — no longer appears among the site's author listings. The Videshi has not independently confirmed the reason for the removal, and Campus Reform's position, if it offers one, will be added to this story.

A conservative who broke ranks

What makes the episode unusual is Bhatt's background. His Campus Reform biography said he previously interned with Senator Ted Cruz's re-election campaign and worked with the Texas Youth Summit, described as one of the largest gatherings of young conservatives in the state. He identified as a conservative; this was not an outside critic being dropped, but a contributor from inside the movement.

Earlier this month, Bhatt drew attention when he said he had voted for Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in Texas's US Senate race. In that earlier statement, reported by hi INDiA's IANS report, he said as a second-generation Indian American he was disgusted by xenophobia, racial resentment and increasingly brazen attacks on his identity, and that his family had contributed to the American story through hard work and sacrifice. "I am every bit as American as anyone else," he said.

The wider argument

Campus Reform is a project of the Leadership Institute, a conservative non-profit based in Virginia that trains young activists, and it uses student correspondents to report on higher education. The dispute has become a flashpoint in a wider argument about hostility toward Indian Americans on the American right, including attacks on Indian-American candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and online abuse aimed at Indian H-1B workers.

Suhag Shukla, executive director of the Hindu American Foundation, criticised the far-right attacks on Bhatt in a personal post on X, linking the climate around them to the period before a foiled plot against a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. Indian-American lawmakers have made a similar argument — that rhetoric of this kind is spilling into violence, citing the Aurora case.

Texas has one of the largest Indian-American populations in the United States, concentrated in Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth, which is why a campus dispute there resonates nationally. For Indian-American students in conservative campus organisations, the practical question Bhatt's case raises is narrow and concrete: whether a contributor role at an advocacy outlet survives a public vote cast against the outlet's own party line. Campus Reform has not answered that question publicly yet.
